content: 1. Patients who are no longer symptomatic but still test positive for COVID-19 can be discharged if they are stable and asymptomatic. 2. Evidence from other viral infections suggests that most individuals who have recovered from COVID-19 and continue to test positive via RT-PCR are unlikely to be infectious. 3. The strength and duration of the immune response after recovery can vary between individuals, with factors such as age potentially influencing immunity. 4. Decisions regarding whether recovered individuals with persistent SARS-CoV-2 RNA detection are infectious and require continued isolation should be made on a case-by-case basis. This determination should consider factors such as medical history, time since the initial positive test, RT-PCR cycle threshold (Ct) values, and the presence of COVID-19 symptoms. 5. If a discharged patient develops new symptoms of COVID-19, they should be isolated and retested. 6. Individuals who test positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR can end isolation after meeting the criteria for either a symptom-based or test-based strategy. 7. It is currently unknown to what extent or for how long a previous COVID-19 infection provides protection against reinfection with SARS-CoV-2. 8. Serologic testing cannot reliably determine whether a person is immune to reinfection. A positive serologic test indicates prior infection but does not confirm immunity. 9. Contact tracing may be necessary if a patient develops new symptoms after discharge, as this could represent a new case of COVID-19. 10. Individuals who have recently recovered from COVID-19 can donate convalescent plasma if they meet blood donation eligibility criteria. 11. Donors must have a documented laboratory-confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19 and meet other laboratory criteria. 12. Donors must have fully recovered from COVID-19, with complete resolution of symptoms for at least 14 days before donating convalescent plasma. 13. Local blood centers can provide information on convalescent plasma donation options. 14. If close contacts of a discharged patient test positive for COVID-19, they should self-isolate and follow quarantine recommendations. 15. It remains unclear to what extent or for how long individuals are protected against reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 after recovering from COVID-19. 16. A positive serologic test may indicate prior infection but does not confirm immunity to reinfection. 17. After discharge, patients should continue wearing face masks in public settings. 18. Cloth face coverings are primarily intended to reduce the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from individuals who may be infectious but asymptomatic or have mild symptoms. 19. Cloth face coverings may also provide some protection to the wearer, offer reassurance to others, and serve as a reminder to maintain social distancing. 20. Cloth face coverings are not personal protective equipment (PPE) and should not replace respirators or medical-grade masks for healthcare workers. 21. Cloth face coverings should not be used by children under the age of 2, individuals with breathing difficulties, or those who are unconscious, incapacitated, or unable to remove the mask without assistance. 22. Patients can return to work after discharge as soon as they feel well enough to do so. They should adhere to strict social distancing, frequent handwashing, face-covering use, and other recommended safety measures. 23. Discharged patients can use public places and transportation but must strictly follow recommended safety measures and guidelines.
